summary: Intro discovery to scope latency and throughput requirements for Zenora's real-time fraud detection streaming use case. Customer evaluating hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments; primary concerns are p95 targets, concurrency (up to ~500 streams), streaming stability and token/sec throughput under 1k concurrent inference requests.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-19 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Maya (Zenora Head of ML), Liam (Infra), Priya (CTO)

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on the account. We also have Ethan, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Maya: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in, we got lots of questions about latency and throughput.
[00:12] Priya: Hi all. We want to understand tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated and private — specifically p95 SLOs and how that scales with concurrency.
[00:20] Ethan: Great. Quick agenda: we'll run through your workload, p95 targets, concurrency/streaming behavior, then share what benchmarking looks like and next steps. Sound good?
[00:26] Liam: Yep. We'll start with current infra.
[00:30] Maya: Quick context — our main product is a streaming real-time fraud detector. We send short prompts per transaction, average prompt length ~65 tokens, responses ~40 tokens. Peak TPS about 1200 transactions per second across regions, but for decisions we fan in to model calls; so practical concurrency for inference is more like 400-600 concurrent model streams, depending on batching.
[00:51] Ethan: Okay that helps. When you say "concurrent model streams" do you mean open streaming websocket sessions, or just concurrent requests?
[00:57] Maya: Both, actually. We use gRPC streams to keep a session open and then send small messages, expect partial streaming output. So streaming latency matters — we need early tokens quickly for partial scoring.
[01:08] Samira: Understood. What are your p95 and p50 targets today?
[01:12] Maya: p95 ideally < 120 ms for first token, p95 end-to-end generation < 400 ms for the 40-token completion. If we can't hit that on hosted, we'd consider dedicated or private.
[01:23] Priya: Security note — if we go private we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. SOC2 is table-stakes.
[01:29] Samira: We're SOC2 compliant; we'll send over the security deck. For KMS/HSM we support customer-managed keys in private and dedicated — we'll include the integration notes.
[01:36] Liam: Our infra: mostly GCP in us-central1 and europe-west1, Kubernetes frontends, we have a pool of GPU inference workers on our side for some experiments but want Redwood to handle scale. Our current baseline with an in-house Llama-based model gives p95 ~280 ms at 300 concurrent streams; scaling to 600 spikes p95 to ~640 ms.
[01:52] Ethan: That's helpful. Two dimensions: latency at your concurrency and the token/sec throughput. For streaming we optimize for first-token latency via warm KV cache and small-batch routing.
[02:04] Maya: Can you explain the difference if we go hosted vs dedicated? In numbers — like what p95 can we expect for 40 tok completions at 500 concurrency?
[02:12] Ethan: With hosted, we have multi-tenant pools optimized for latency; you'll get good single-digit 100s p95 for small completions at moderate concurrency, but at very high sustained concurrency we suggest Dedicated so you get reserved capacity and predictable p95. Typical numbers we see: on Dedicated with A100-like capacity and optimized kernel selection, p95 for 40-token completion at 500 concurrent streaming sessions can be around 250–350 ms depending on model variant and quantization. Hosted can be similar during non-peak but can vary under noisy neighbors.
[02:44] Priya: What about token/sec benchmarks — how do you measure and what's realistic per-GPU?
[02:49] Ethan: We report tokens/sec tail percentiles per model/instance type. For example, an 8-bit quantized 7B model on an A2-equivalent may do X tokens/sec; larger models drop. We'll share a benchmark sheet. For your workload (short prompts, streaming partials), effective tokens/sec is impacted by network lat, batch size, and KV cache hit rates.
[03:06] Maya: KV cache — we have a lot of prefix overlap since transactions share templates. How much does caching help?
[03:11] Ethan: Substantial. With good prefix cache hit rates you can drop per-request computation a lot, improving p95 by 20–40% in many cases. We automatically manage caching and can pin cache policies per-route.
[03:23] Liam: For the 1k concurrent spike scenario, do you recommend autoscaling or reserved burst capacity?
[03:29] Samira: Reserved Dedicated with burst buffer is typical: commit to baseline for cost predictability and allow burst capacity to handle spikes. For private deployments you control autoscaling but need to size GPUs.
[03:38] Priya: Can we run a POC where Redwood runs a benchmark against our sample workload?
[03:42] Samira: Absolutely. Ethan will pod the harness. We'll need a representative prompt set, expected concurrency curves, and desired SLOs.
[03:49] Ethan: For benchmarking we'll provide a script that simulates streaming sessions, measures first-token and complete generation p95/p50, and reports token/sec under load. We'll also include guidance to run in your env if you prefer private testing.
[04:01] Maya: What about cold starts and model warm-up? We need predictable first-token latency after deploys.
[04:06] Ethan: We do pre-warming and keep a small pool warm for Dedicated. For hosted we have warm pools and can pin model instances for premium tiers. We also support continuous batching so tail variation is reduced. Cold starts can spike, but we recommend canary rollouts with pinned warmers.
[04:20] Liam: Any thoughts on quantization vs model size? We're considering moving from 13B to a quantized 7B if it keeps accuracy.
[04:26] Ethan: Quantization reduces tokens/sec compute and memory; it usually improves throughput with minor quality tradeoffs. Our optimize toolkit suggests quantization profiles by workload — we'll include recommendations.
[04:35] Maya: Pricing is a factor — can you give ballpark per-token or per-hour numbers for Dedicated baseline?
[04:40] Samira: I'll send detailed pricing. Ballpark: Dedicated reserved nodes priced by GPU-hour + model licensing; effective per-token depends on batch rates and caching. We'll provide example unit economics using your sample traffic.
[04:51] Priya: On security — logs and residency. We need logs retained 1 year and EU-only data residency for EU traffic.
[04:58] Samira: We support region routing and retention configurations; for Private you control full residency. For hosted we can route EU traffic to europe-west1 pools and set log retention per account. We'll include compliance docs.
[05:12] Ethan: Quick technical note on measuring p95: the benchmark harness reports both server-side token latency and end-to-end wall clock latency including network. We recommend focusing on server-side for infra comparisons but end-to-end matters for your product.
[05:26] Maya: If we hit p95 failures in production, what's the degradation path?
[05:30] Ethan: We have automatic fallback policies — route to a lower-cost variant or fall back to cached responses; canary rollouts and autoscaling alerts. For Dedicated we have guaranteed capacity to reduce noisy neighbor impact.
[05:42] Liam: For the POC, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[05:45] Ethan: Sample prompts, expected concurrency profile (time series), network RTTs from frontends to candidate regions, and any policy on tokenization (e.g., special tokens).
[05:54] Maya: We'll prepare a dataset of 2k representative transactions and an hourly concurrency curve.
[05:58] Samira: Great. Recap and next steps: I'll send pricing/security; Ethan will send the benchmark harness and config; Liam will share telemetry. We'll target a 1-week turnaround to run the initial benchmark.
[06:10] Priya: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[06:13] Maya: One more — how do you surface per-route p95 in the console?
[06:17] Ethan: Per-route dashboards in Redwood Console with token-level breakdown, latency histograms and trace links. We'll share screenshots.
[06:25] Samira: OK we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.
[06:28] Maya: Thanks.
[06:30] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional overlap and filler words; some product names transcribed as "KV cache" and "k v cache" interchangeably.
